messages.content:
## Responses as Code

Each turn, you take your turn by calling the `submit_program` tool. Its `program`
string is run as one Swift program: pass one whole, legal
Swift program — bare code, with no code fences around it and no
prose inside it — and it is processed exactly as written. All calls are
synchronous.

`submit_program` is the only tool in this session, and every reply must call it.
Each call is acknowledged with a tool result reading `ok`; what the program
produced arrives as separate messages after it. Text you write alongside the
call is recorded, but nothing reads code out of it: only the `program` string
runs. If one reply makes several `submit_program` calls, the programs run
sequentially, in order, every one of them.

Your program is compiled by `swiftc` before it runs. A program it refuses
is not executed: you get its diagnostics and submit another program.

## Views

Views are the only way to read data out of your code and are provided on the
turn after they're opened. Print statements are not shown.

Reading images is not supported.

## Language Rules

Your program is compiled verbatim, as a whole Swift file. It is the top level of
a program, so bare statements run in the order you wrote them.

## Ending your session

Turns continue until you end your session.

A program that fails does not end your session: the ending it called is revoked.
Fix the fault and end your session in a program that runs to completion.

Call `gg.session.finish` with a short summary of what you did once the work is
complete.

## Your modules

Your program is given these modules:

- `gg.files`: Read, write, edit, list and search the files of the workspace. — brought into scope with `import gg`
- `gg.shell`: Run shell commands in the workspace. — brought into scope with `import gg`
- `gg.views`: Show a file, a computed value, or an entry's documentation. — brought into scope with `import gg`
- `gg.docs`: Find the modules, functions and types this run bound, and take their documentation back out of context. — brought into scope with `import gg`
- `gg.session`: End the session, with the ending that belongs to this agent's role. — brought into scope with `import gg`

Search the documentation to find a function, by keyword or by naming modules
above. Open a documentation view of each function you intend to call, and write
the call on a later turn.

The SDK declares every function, whatever this run enabled, so a call to one this
run withheld compiles and then fails when it runs, naming the call. What you can
find in the documentation is what you can call.

## Messages you receive

Every message you receive is headed by one of the following labels, on its own
line — a view's label is followed by `: ` and the name it was opened under; a
file view's by `: `, its path, `:`, the 1-based inclusive line range shown and
the file's total line count — followed by a `----` rule and then the content:

- `Task` — the task you are working on, or a message from a parent agent
- `Compiler error` — your last program did not compile, so none of it ran; the message is the compiler's error and nothing else. Fix it and resend the whole program
- `Runtime error` — your last program compiled and then threw, or was stopped by a sandbox limit; the message is the error and nothing else. Whatever the program did before it threw stands, so do not repeat that work
- `Notice` — a process notice from the harness (a mode change, or guidance)
- `Summary` — a summary standing in for older turns the harness compacted out of the window
- `Documentation` — documentation or a skill you asked to read, delivered on the following turn
- `File` — a file, or a window of one, shown in your context — seeded by the run or opened by your own file-view call — headed by its path, the 1-based line range shown and the file's total line count, as `File: src/main.ts:100-250 of 400 lines` (a whole file's range runs `1-N`)
- `View` — a value your program put into your window; the view's label follows the heading, as `View: changed-files`

For example, lines 100 to 250 of a 400-line file you opened a view of arrive
as:

```
File: src/main.ts:100-250 of 400 lines
----
...those lines of the file...
```

A program that ran is not announced: the views it opened are the result.

Task
----
Create the file `notes/plan.md` in the workspace. Its required content is specified in `specs/plan-brief.md`, which is already open in your context. Write the file exactly as the brief specifies.

Documentation: gg.docs.search
----
search(query: String? = nil, modules: [String] = [], type: String? = nil, kind: docs.DocKind? = nil, offset: Int? = nil, limit: Int? = nil) throws -> docs.DocSearch
  query?: String? = nil — The words to look for, matched as case-insensitive substrings. Several specific words rank an entry above one vague word. Left out, the filters are the whole of the search.
  modules?: [String] = [] — The modules to look in, each by gg's id (`files`) or by this arm's path (`gg.files`). Exact and case-insensitive, because a module filter is a lookup rather than a search, and several are a **union**: an entry in any one of them is a hit, and modules with no query at all are those modules' whole directory. Empty, which is the default, is no module filter and every module searched.
  type?: String? = nil — One type's own name (`FileRead`), narrowing to it and to every function whose signature mentions it — what a value of this shape can be used for. Left out, nothing is narrowed.
  kind?: docs.DocKind? = nil — Whether to return only modules, only functions or only types. Left out, all three come back.
  offset?: Int? = nil — How many hits to skip, for paging through a total larger than one page. Left out, the page starts at the best match.
  limit?: Int? = nil — How many hits to return. Left out, the page holds 20; the ceiling is 100, and a larger one clamps rather than failing.

Defined in `gg.docs`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

Search the bound modules, functions and types by keyword, by module, or by both — best match first.

Matching is case-insensitive substring over names, signatures, briefs and detailed descriptions, so `docs` finds `openDocsView` and `view` finds every call that mentions one. Ranking is by the kind of evidence that matched: an entry whose own name matched outranks one that merely mentions the word in a paragraph, however often it mentions it. Only what this run bound is ever returned, so nothing a search finds is something the program cannot call.

The result is a value and a view. The value is readable in the turn that asked for it; the view puts the same page in the next prompt under the selector `search results`, replaced by the next search rather than accumulating. A hit carries a brief and no more — reading one in full is `views.openDocsView` on its `key`.

Every argument has a default, so a call may be words alone, filters alone, or both. The one shape it refuses is the empty one: no query and no filter is a call that asked for nothing, which is a different answer from a call that matched nothing.

- Returns: the page that matched, best first, and how many matched behind it.
- Throws: `core.ApiError` with `.invalidArgument` when there is no query and no filter at all — asking for nothing and matching nothing are different answers — and when `limit` is `0`, which is a page that could never answer anything.

Documentation: gg.views.openFile
----
openFile(_ path: String, offset: Int? = nil, limit: Int? = nil, maxLineChars: Int? = nil) throws -> files.FileRead
  path: String — The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.
  offset?: Int? = nil — The 1-based line to start at. Left out, the whole file is shown.
  limit?: Int? = nil — How many lines to show from `offset`. Left out, the view runs to the end.
  maxLineChars?: Int? = nil — Cut each line of the view longer than this many characters, annotating it in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`; `1...65536`. Left out, every line arrives whole.

Defined in `gg.views`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

Read a file and place it in the context window, attributed to its path and filed under it.

What comes back is exactly what `files.readFile` returns; the difference is the view. That split is the point: reading gets bytes for the program, opening shows the file to the agent, so a program that reads forty files to grep them puts nothing in the window. `offset` and `limit` select a window of lines, and two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate. An image is shown as a picture, and this is the only call that shows one.

The view's text body is held to the same 65,536-byte cap a text view's body is: a window that would carry more is refused, naming the size and the bound, and nothing is opened — never a truncation. The program narrows the window with `offset` and `limit`, or cuts the file's long lines with `maxLineChars`: given, each line of the *view* longer than that many characters is cut there and annotated in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`, with the count of characters dropped. The cut is the view's alone — the value this returns and the file itself are untouched — and the cap is measured against the body after it. Left out, lines arrive whole.

- Returns: exactly what `files.readFile` returns for the same file, long lines and all.
- Throws: `core.ApiError` with `.notFound` for a missing path, `.invalidArgument` for an offset past the end of the file or a `maxLineChars` outside `1...65536`, and `.limitExceeded` — naming the size and the bound — for a text body over 65,536 bytes after the cut. The read is what fails; nothing is opened when it does.

Documentation: gg.files.FileRead
----
enum FileRead { case text(files.TextFile); case image(files.ImageFile) }

Defined in `gg.files`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

What a read returned: a text file's window, or a picture's description.

A picture is a different kind of thing from text, so it is a different case rather than a string that happens to be binary — a program that treats an image as text is caught by the `switch` instead of silently writing an empty string somewhere. Image bytes never enter the program: gg attaches the picture to the turn instead, which is worth far more than base64 in a variable.
  text: files.TextFile — This file is text.
  image: files.ImageFile — This file is a picture, which gg shows rather than handing over its bytes.

  path: String — Where to write, relative to the workspace or absolute. Parent directories are created.
  contents: String — The UTF-8 text to write. It replaces the file entirely.

Defined in `gg.files`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

Write UTF-8 text to a file, creating parent directories and replacing what is there.

- Returns: how many bytes were written.
- Throws: `core.ApiError` with `.invalidArgument` for an empty path, and `.ioError` when creating the parent directories or the write itself failed.

openFile(_ path: String, offset: Int? = nil, limit: Int? = nil, maxLineChars: Int? = nil) throws -> files.FileRead
  path: String — The file to open, relative to the workspace or absolute.
  offset?: Int? = nil — The 1-based line to start at. Left out, the whole file is shown.

Defined in `gg.views`, brought into scope with `import gg`.

Read a file and place it in the context window, attributed to its path and filed under it.

What comes back is exactly what `files.readFile` returns; the difference is the view. That split is the point: reading gets bytes for the program, opening shows the file to the agent, so a program that reads forty files to grep them puts nothing in the window. `offset` and `limit` select a window of lines, and two pages of one file are two views that coexist; re-opening the same page replaces what it showed rather than piling up a duplicate. An image is shown as a picture, and this is the only call that shows one.

The view's text body is held to the same 65,536-byte cap a text view's body is: a window that would carry more is refused, naming the size and the bound, and nothing is opened — never a truncation. The program narrows the window with `offset` and `limit`, or cuts the file's long lines with `maxLineChars`: given, each line of the *view* longer than that many characters is cut there and annotated in place as `foo (123 more chars...)`, with the count of characters dropped. The cut is the view's alone — the value this returns and the file itself are untouched — and the cap is measured against the body after it. Left out, lines arrive whole.

- Returns: exactly what `files.readFile` returns for the same file, long lines and all.
- Throws: `core.ApiError` with `.notFound` for a missing path, `.invalidArgument` for an offset past the end of the file or a `maxLineChars` outside `1...65536`, and `.limitExceeded` — naming the size and the bound — for a text body over 65,536 bytes after the cut. The read is what fails; nothing is opened when it does.

What a read returned: a text file's window, or a picture's description.

A picture is a different kind of thing from text, so it is a different case rather than a string that happens to be binary — a program that treats an image as text is caught by the `switch` instead of silently writing an empty string somewhere. Image bytes never enter the program: gg attaches the picture to the turn instead, which is worth far more than base64 in a variable.
